briefing.text: Before any testing, establish which disease and cohort these tables actually cover. Tabulate CANCER_TYPE, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED and ONCOTREE_CODE in data_clinical_sample.txt and search all clinical and mutation files for thyroid codes and terms (THPA, THAP, ATC, PDTC, 'anaplastic', 'thyroid'). Library inspection reported the cohort to be dominated by non-small cell lung cancer on lung cfDNA/IMPACT panels, with the only 'Thyroid' string appearing as a METASTATIC_SITE value, not as a tumour type. A metastatic-site value is not a primary tumour type, and lung subgroups are not a stand-in for thyroid histologies. Check this yourself, then apply the task's labelling convention to whatever you find.
briefing.reason: Whether the hypothesis concerns this study's cancer type decides which part of the labelling convention applies. Teams must verify the cohort first rather than mapping a thyroid claim onto unrelated subgroups.

briefing.text: Mutational-signature decomposition (SBS96 refitting) is unreliable on targeted panels, which usually yield fewer than about 10 SNVs per sample. If any signature-style comparison is attempted, count SNVs per sample and check panel size per GENE_PANEL. With low counts, pool by group, limit refitting to dominant signatures (SBS1, SBS2/13, SBS4) or compare simple spectra (such as C>A fraction) with bootstrapping.
briefing.reason: This affects how a signature claim can validly be tested on panel data, if relevant groups exist.

briefing.text: Some patients contribute several samples (tissue plus cfDNA, serial draws). Count SAMPLE_IDs per PATIENT_ID, and collapse to one sample per patient or use patient-level models before comparing groups.
briefing.reason: Pseudoreplication inflates n and duplicates mutations, which biases any group comparison.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that tumour type is captured by CANCER_TYPE/ONCOTREE_CODE and that no undiagnosed thyroid tumours hide among CUP/PDC/UDMN samples. I checked this: the 4 PDC, 1 UDMN and 1 MT samples all have PRIMARY_SITE 'Unknown', and no PRIMARY_SITE is thyroid. The only 'Neck' primary is an oral cavity SCC.

Both teams assumed the benchmark convention (an off-cohort hypothesis is Not verifiable) applies. The data clearly support that this is an NSCLC cfDNA/IMPACT cohort with 2539 of about 2620 samples NSCLC.
unused_evidence: PRIMARY_SITE and patient HISTOLOGY were not cited by either team. I checked both: no thyroid entry in either (HISTOLOGY is Adenocarcinoma/Squamous/Other).
THYC (3 samples) is thymic carcinoma, not thyroid. Neither team mistook it for thyroid, and it does not bear on ATC vs other thyroid cancers.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A's weakest point is reliance on the labelling convention. That is inherent to the task and is consistent with the data, which hold zero thyroid primaries, so no ATC vs non-ATC comparison is possible. Team B reported no weak point.
second_readings: 'Other thyroid cancers' could be read as comparing ATC with non-thyroid cancers. Even on that reading, the data contain no anaplastic thyroid samples, so no reading makes the hypothesis about this cohort.
challenge.verdict: High trust in 'Not verifiable'. I checked CANCER_TYPE, ONCOTREE_CODE, PRIMARY_SITE, HISTOLOGY and a text search, and the cohort contains no thyroid tumours of any kind, anaplastic or otherwise. The hypothesis concerns a disease these tables do not cover, which is exactly the benchmark's Not verifiable case, so I have no question that could change the method.
